prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: whether the home policy covers flooding. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When the claimant says ‘flood’, check whether the water came from an external source, such as heavy rainfall, river overflow or surface water, because that is usually within home cover if flood is included in the policy schedule."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the policy schedule or certificate shows flood cover is excluded, I do not assume any exception applies until I have checked for separate endorsements or extensions that might restore cover."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the water entered through doors, air bricks, vents or a lowered threshold during widespread rainfall, I treat it differently from a leak or internal escape of water, because the source and cause drive the cover decision."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the damage is from groundwater, river overflow or surface water and the insured peril includes flood, I can usually confirm the event is covered subject to the normal excess, limits and any relevant conditions."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the report mentions sewer backing up or drains overflowing, I check whether the policy has a specific extension for flood or for accidental damage from water, because not every drainage event is classed as flood cover."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the weather has been severe, I prefer to cross-check the claim against Met Office alerts and local incident reports, because that helps me separate a genuine flood event from an isolated internal leak."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the property is on a hillside or away from obvious watercourses, I do not rule out flood too quickly, because surface water can still run downhill and enter the home even where river flood is unlikely."},{"type":"fact","content":"When flood is covered, I still look for policy conditions about maintenance, immediate loss mitigation and temporary protection, because failing to act reasonably after ingress can affect what we can pay."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the member describes repeated damp or long-term seepage rather than sudden ingress, I treat that as a potential non-flood issue, since gradual wear, poor maintenance or rising damp is usually handled differently."},{"type":"fact","content":"When there is any uncertainty about the cause, I record the claim as needing further validation rather than declining cover early, because the difference between flood and another water peril can change the decision completely."}]}
